title: Who gets the proceeds from the AI listing wave?
summary: A billion dollars of shares sold to the public can finance a company’s next investment, pay an early shareholder for taking risk years ago, or do some of each. Only the first use puts new loss-absorbing capital on the company’s balance sheet. Both can increase the shares available to index investors. Daniel Dieckelmann, Lavinia Franco, Paraic O’Gorman and Chiara Scommegna use that distinction to examine what the US listing boom means for financing and for euro area investors. They judge the direct stability risk from issuance to be limited. The risk grows if borrowers accumulate debt and then lose access to equity funding.

Chart C.1 distinguishes completed offerings from prospective ones. By the 10 November information cutoff, SpaceX had listed, Anthropic had filed an amended registration statement but had yet to trade, and OpenAI’s listing was expected in 2027. A July market estimate put 2026 US IPO proceeds at $225 billion, compared with about $44 billion in 2025. The ECB’s later estimate of $212 billion combined January–October proceeds, historical seasonality for the final two months and a separate allowance for Anthropic (Chart C.3). Both annual estimates depend on unusually large deals. The separate series on net public issuance deducts repurchases and ends in the second quarter. Gross IPO proceeds alone cannot establish that the US corporate sector became a net issuer for the year.

Private capital now allows firms to grow larger before listing. Chart C.2 compares venture financing and age at IPO with successive private valuations of three technology companies. Going public makes a price continuously visible and transfers some risk from venture investors to new shareholders. The authors report that 76% of IPO offerings in 2023–26 were primary. A primary tranche creates new shares and puts cash in the business. A secondary tranche pays a selling shareholder. Either can expand free float, but only capital actually raised by the issuer can fund investment or pay down its debt.

Chart C.4 relates IPO proceeds as a share of GDP to market returns over the next two years. The fitted relationship slopes down in both markets but explains only 10.5% of variation in US returns and 5.3% in the euro area. For IPOs of at least €1 billion, the reported one-month median return was 5.0% against 1.0% for the market. At one year the comparison reversed to 7.6% against 9.7%. The issuer sample comes from past and present index constituents. Lower discount rates, better expected investment opportunities and issuers anticipating a closing market window could all affect timing. Chart C.3 compares index earnings yields with ten-year government bond yields. An earnings yield is an accounting ratio, not an observed required equity return.

Passive funds that track float-adjusted indices may need to buy when an offering raises a company’s index weight. Since passive ownership can only be observed after listing, Chart C.5 tests this mechanism on follow-on offerings. The sample includes 1,990 current or former US and euro area index constituents, with passive ownership data from January 2014 to July 2026. Increases in passive ownership over twelve months are associated with a higher probability of a follow-on offering over the same period. Among firms that actually issued shares, one percentage point more passive ownership a month earlier is associated with an offering about 3% larger, controlling for firm characteristics and time effects. Falling passive ownership was much less common and had a weaker relationship with issuance.

For IPOs, the authors cite separate research finding that firms expecting rapid index inclusion raised around 6% more capital than comparable listings. The relative price advantage disappeared within roughly three weeks of inclusion. A temporary price premium thus says little about longer-run funding costs. Europe had no comparable IPO boom, but its investors hold US equities. Concentrated household ownership limits the likely consumption effect of a correction. The more consequential channel could be issuers’ ability to finance capital spending if both equity demand and creditors’ confidence weaken. A deeper European public equity market could broaden sources of risk-bearing capital. Its resilience would still depend on whether demand endures through a downturn.

questions.question: How much cash from each large offering actually funds the company?
questions.detail: Separate primary and secondary tranches, trace primary proceeds to investment or debt repayment, and compare them with scheduled repayments and contracted spending. A large float increase accompanying little new issuer capital would matter for index demand and the distribution of losses, but say little about resilience to a funding squeeze.

questions.question: Does faster index entry change the quantity of capital raised or merely the price at entry?
questions.detail: Compare similarly sized issuers qualifying under different index rules and follow primary proceeds, insider sales and prices beyond the three-week reversal window cited in the article. Eligibility itself depends on size, liquidity and float. Accounting for those features is essential before attributing any remaining difference to passive demand.

questions.question: When does high issuance add information about subsequent returns?
questions.detail: Repeat the two-year comparison with the largest listings removed and with starting earnings yields, credit yields and funding conditions observed at the time. This would test whether the relationship survives the influence of a few mega-deals and whether a plausible change in discount rates can account for it without an exuberance explanation.

questions.question: Which European exposures would turn a US equity correction into a financing problem?
questions.detail: Distinguish mark-to-market losses for well-capitalised holders from debt or commitments payable before operating cash flows arrive. Pair that schedule with evidence on whether euro area issuers could still raise primary equity under weaker fund flows. Losses on existing shares and the disappearance of funding for new investment have different economic consequences.
